emt-medical-l01.q: A conscious, cooperative patient in severe pulmonary edema has a blood pressure of 78/50. Should you apply CPAP?
choices: Yes, CPAP at 5 to 10 cm H2O is indicated for any pulmonary edema patient
No, hypotension is a contraindication because CPAP further reduces venous return and can drop the pressure further
Yes, but only after intubation
No, because CPAP is never used in pulmonary edema
emt-medical-l01.why: CPAP increases intrathoracic pressure, which reduces the blood returning to the heart, so a hypotensive patient can be driven into worse shock. CPAP is not a substitute for intubation and it is in fact the first-line BLS tool for pulmonary edema in a patient with an adequate pressure, so the last two choices are wrong for opposite reasons.

emt-medical-l01.q: A patient with a metered-dose albuterol inhaler has no spacer available. Why does that matter?
choices: It does not matter; the spacer is only for pediatric patients
Without a spacer, most of the dose lands in the mouth and throat instead of the lungs, so far less drug reaches the airway
Without a spacer the inhaler will not release medication at all
The spacer prevents the tremor and tachycardia the drug normally causes
emt-medical-l01.why: A spacer holds the aerosol in a chamber so the patient can inhale it slowly and deeply instead of most of it hitting the back of the throat, which happens with direct inhaler use regardless of age. The device still fires without a spacer, and tremor and tachycardia are expected beta-2 effects that a spacer does not block.

emt-medical-l02.q: A woman eats a food containing tree nuts and develops hives and itching on her arms only, with normal breathing, normal blood pressure, and no other symptoms. What is this?
choices: Anaphylaxis, because any exposure to a known allergen requires epinephrine
A localized allergic reaction, since only one body system is involved and there is no hypotension
Anaphylaxis, because hives are always a systemic finding
A toxidrome requiring naloxone
emt-medical-l02.why: One system involved, with no respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal findings, is a limited allergic reaction rather than anaphylaxis, which requires two or more systems or hypotension after exposure. Epinephrine is not indicated here, and naloxone has nothing to do with an allergic reaction.

emt-medical-l02.q: How does epinephrine reverse the effects of an anaphylactic reaction?
choices: It blocks histamine receptors directly, the same as an antihistamine
Alpha-1 stimulation constricts vessels and shrinks swelling, beta-1 raises heart rate and contractility, and beta-2 opens the bronchi, reversing all three histamine effects at once
It sedates the patient so the allergic response cannot be felt
It only treats the skin findings such as hives
emt-medical-l02.why: Epinephrine works through adrenergic receptors, not by blocking histamine, which is what an antihistamine does. It raises blood pressure, opens the airway, and reduces swelling simultaneously rather than only masking symptoms or targeting the skin alone.

emt-medical-l03.q: Why does BE-FAST add balance and eyes to the older FAST stroke screen?
choices: Because balance and eye symptoms are the most common stroke presentation overall
Because they catch posterior circulation strokes that a face, arm, and speech exam alone can miss
Because balance testing replaces the need to check glucose
Because eye symptoms confirm a hemorrhagic rather than ischemic stroke
emt-medical-l03.why: Sudden loss of balance or vision can be the only sign of a stroke affecting the back of the brain, which the original face, arm, and speech items do not test for. Balance testing does not substitute for a glucose check, and eye symptoms do not tell you ischemic from hemorrhagic, which cannot be determined in the field either way.

emt-medical-l03.q: A patient's last known well was 5 hours ago with a clear-cut stroke presentation. Is she automatically excluded from all acute stroke treatment?
choices: Yes, all stroke treatment requires last known well within 4.5 hours
Yes, because thrombectomy is limited to 3 hours
No, she is past the 4.5-hour thrombolytic window but may still qualify for thrombectomy, which can extend to 24 hours in selected large-vessel strokes
No, there is no time limit for any stroke treatment
emt-medical-l03.why: Thrombolytics are generally limited to 4.5 hours, but thrombectomy for a large-vessel occlusion can be offered out to 24 hours in eligible patients based on imaging, so she is not automatically excluded from everything. This is exactly why destination and early notification still matter past the thrombolytic window, and claiming no time limit exists at all ignores the thrombolytic cutoff that does apply.

emt-medical-l04.q: A 55-year-old describes a headache that reached maximal intensity within seconds, calling it the worst of her life, with vomiting and neck stiffness. What should you suspect and do?
choices: A migraine; give a dark quiet ride and no further action is needed
A tension headache from stress; reassure and transport routinely
Possible subarachnoid hemorrhage; treat as a time-critical neurologic emergency
A sinus infection; recommend she see her primary doctor
emt-medical-l04.why: A thunderclap headache that peaks within seconds, especially with vomiting and neck stiffness, is a classic subarachnoid hemorrhage presentation and needs urgent transport and reassessment, not reassurance. Migraine and tension headaches build up rather than hitting maximal intensity instantly, and a sinus infection does not present this way.

emt-medical-l04.q: During the clonic phase of a generalized tonic-clonic seizure, where is tongue biting typically found, and what should you do about it?
choices: On the tip of the tongue, and you should place a padded tongue depressor to prevent it
On the side of the tongue, and nothing should be placed in the mouth
It does not occur during a true seizure
On the tip of the tongue, and suction should be withheld until the seizure ends
emt-medical-l04.why: Side-of-tongue biting is typical during the rhythmic jerking of the clonic phase, and nothing goes in the mouth of a seizing patient because objects break teeth and get aspirated. Tongue biting does happen in real seizures, and suction should be available and used as needed rather than deliberately withheld.

emt-medical-l05.q: An 84-year-old is profoundly confused and severely dehydrated with a glucose reading of 640 mg/dL. Her breathing is normal, not deep or rapid, and there is no fruity odor. What does the absence of Kussmaul breathing suggest?
choices: This still fits classic diabetic ketoacidosis and Kussmaul breathing was simply missed
This pattern fits hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, which lacks significant ketosis despite an even higher glucose
This means her glucose reading is inaccurate
This means she is actually hypoglycemic and the meter malfunctioned
emt-medical-l05.why: HHS produces extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration in older type 2 patients without the significant ketone production that drives Kussmaul respirations and fruity breath in DKA. A missing hallmark finding is a real diagnostic clue rather than something to assume was overlooked, and nothing here suggests either a faulty reading or hypoglycemia, which would show a low number.

emt-medical-l05.q: Fifteen minutes after one tube of oral glucose, a hypoglycemic patient's recheck reads 68 mg/dL and he remains mildly confused but is swallowing well. What is the next step under the rule of 15?
choices: Repeat oral glucose 15 g and recheck again in 15 minutes
Give glucagon intramuscularly instead since one dose already failed
Do nothing further since he improved slightly
Restrict oral intake since he is still confused
emt-medical-l05.why: The rule of 15 repeats a 15 g dose and rechecks every 15 minutes until the patient is above target and improving, and 68 mg/dL with ongoing symptoms has not cleared that bar. Glucagon is reserved for a patient who cannot swallow, which he still can, and stopping treatment on a still-confused, still-low patient abandons him mid-course.

emt-medical-l06.q: A patient with right upper quadrant pain that began 40 minutes after a fatty meal also reports pain radiating to the right shoulder blade. What does the referred pain suggest?
choices: A kidney stone, since flank pain often radiates
Gallbladder irritation, since gallbladder pain classically refers to the right shoulder blade
A pulmonary embolism
Nothing significant; referred pain is not clinically useful
emt-medical-l06.why: Shared nerve pathways send gallbladder pain to the right shoulder blade, and the timing after a fatty meal reinforces cholecystitis or biliary colic. Kidney stone pain classically refers to the groin rather than the shoulder, a pulmonary embolism does not produce postprandial right upper quadrant pain, and referred pain patterns are one of the more useful clues in an abdominal exam, not a distraction.

emt-medical-l06.q: A patient has been vomiting blood that looks like coffee grounds rather than bright red. What does this appearance indicate?
choices: Active brisk upper gastrointestinal bleeding
Slower upper gastrointestinal bleeding where blood has been altered by stomach acid
Lower gastrointestinal bleeding
A bleeding disorder rather than a structural GI source
emt-medical-l06.why: Coffee-ground emesis is blood that has sat in stomach acid long enough to be partially digested, which points to a slower upper GI bleed rather than a brisk, actively bleeding one. Bright red vomited blood, not coffee-ground, indicates active bleeding, and this finding describes a location rather than proving any specific underlying disorder.

emt-medical-l07.q: A patient who used methamphetamine is agitated, paranoid, sweating heavily, with a temperature of 40.1 C and a heart rate of 152. What is the treatment priority?
choices: Give naloxone to reverse the stimulant
Actively cool the patient, keep the environment calm and dim, and treat any chest pain seriously
Restrain aggressively and place him prone to control the agitation
Withhold oxygen since his breathing rate is already elevated
emt-medical-l07.why: Hyperthermia, dysrhythmia, and stroke are the real dangers in stimulant toxicity, so active cooling and a calm approach matter most, along with taking any chest pain seriously since stimulants cause real coronary spasm. Naloxone does nothing for a stimulant, prone restraint risks positional asphyxia in an already hyperthermic tachycardic patient, and oxygen is not withheld based on respiratory rate alone.

emt-medical-l07.q: A patient who combined alprazolam with alcohol is unresponsive with slow shallow breathing and normal-sized pupils. Naloxone is given with no effect. What should you conclude and do?
choices: The naloxone dose was too low; give repeated doses until there is a response
This is a sedative-alcohol combination, which naloxone does not reverse; manage the airway and ventilate
This confirms an opioid overdose that simply needs more time
This means the patient is faking unresponsiveness
emt-medical-l07.why: Naloxone only reverses opioids, and normal pupils plus a sedative-alcohol combination explain why it did nothing here; the correct move is airway management and ventilation, not repeated naloxone. Pinpoint pupils would be expected with an opioid, and there is no basis here for assuming the patient is faking unresponsiveness.

emt-medical-l08.q: A toddler swallowed drain cleaner 15 minutes ago and is crying with visible burns around the mouth. Medical direction is reached. What is correct?
choices: Give activated charcoal since it is within the one-hour window
Give water or milk to dilute the caustic before transport
Do not give charcoal or attempt to dilute or neutralize the substance; treat the airway as the emergency and transport
Induce vomiting to remove the remaining substance
emt-medical-l08.why: Charcoal obscures endoscopy and does not help caustic burns that have already occurred, and diluting or neutralizing is avoided unless medical direction specifically orders it, since it can cause more injury. The airway is the true emergency in caustic ingestion because of swelling, and inducing vomiting re-exposes already burned tissue to the caustic agent.

emt-medical-l08.q: A 70 kg adult swallowed a large number of tablets 30 minutes ago and is fully alert. Medical direction orders activated charcoal. Which dose and timing consideration is correct?
choices: Roughly 1 g/kg, so about 50 to 70 g, given now since it is within about an hour of ingestion
A fixed 10 g dose regardless of weight, given any time within 24 hours
Charcoal should be withheld because the patient is alert
Charcoal is dosed at 1 mg/kg and works best after 4 hours
emt-medical-l08.why: The charcoal dose is roughly 1 g/kg, which for a 70 kg adult falls in the usual 25 to 50 g adult range or scales up toward 70 g, and it is most useful within about an hour of ingestion. Being alert enough to protect the airway is a requirement for giving charcoal, not a reason to withhold it, and the dose is not a fixed amount or a milligram-scale figure.

emt-medical-l09.q: A landscaper working in the heat develops painful muscle spasms in his calves. He is alert, his skin is sweaty but not unusually hot, and he has no confusion. What is this and what do you do?
choices: Heat cramps; move him to a cool place, rest, and give oral electrolyte fluid if alert
Heat stroke; begin aggressive cold-water immersion immediately
Heat exhaustion; withhold fluids until his vitals stabilize
A seizure secondary to hyperthermia
emt-medical-l09.why: Painful spasms with normal mentation and no significant temperature elevation describe heat cramps, which are managed with rest, cooling, and oral fluids rather than aggressive cooling reserved for heat stroke. He is not altered, so this is not heat exhaustion or stroke, and nothing here describes a seizure.

emt-medical-l09.q: A hiker has frostbite of several toes and a long transport time ahead with no risk of refreezing. What is appropriate field care?
choices: Vigorously rub the toes to restore circulation before transport
Rewarm using circulating water around 99 to 102 F if appropriate, then cover with dry sterile dressings and separate the digits
Apply direct dry heat such as a heating pad to speed rewarming
Pop any blisters that form to relieve pressure
emt-medical-l09.why: Rubbing shreds already damaged, ice-crystal-filled tissue, and controlled water at 99 to 102 F is the correct rewarming temperature when refreezing will not occur, followed by dry sterile dressings with digits separated. Direct dry heat sources like heating pads risk burning numb tissue the patient cannot feel, and blisters are not opened in the field.

emt-medical-l10.q: A patient tells you she has been feeling hopeless. What is the correct way to assess for suicide risk?
choices: Avoid the topic entirely to prevent giving her the idea
Ask directly whether she is thinking about killing herself and whether she has a plan
Ask only vague, indirect questions about her mood
Wait for her to bring it up on her own before asking anything
emt-medical-l10.why: Asking directly about suicidal thoughts and a specific plan does not plant the idea and is the only reliable way to assess risk, with a specific plan and available means raising concern further. Avoiding the topic or only asking indirectly leaves real risk unassessed, and waiting for the patient to volunteer it lets a dangerous situation go unrecognized.

emt-medical-l10.q: A combative patient with unusual strength and a temperature of 40.3 C suddenly stops fighting and becomes calm and quiet after a prolonged struggle. What does this most likely mean?
choices: The de-escalation worked and he is now safe to transport without further concern
He is exhausted but stable and simply needs rest
This is a pre-arrest warning sign in excited delirium, and monitoring must intensify rather than relax
He is faking calmness to avoid restraints
emt-medical-l10.why: Sudden calm after violent struggle in excited or hyperactive delirium is a known warning that cardiac arrest may be imminent, so vigilance and monitoring should increase, not decrease. Treating this as resolution or simple exhaustion, or assuming manipulation, all risk missing the point at which these patients most often arrest.

emt-medical-l11.q: A patient with distended neck veins, bilateral pitting edema, a furosemide prescription, and wheezing on exam asks why albuterol alone will not fix her breathing. What is the explanation?
choices: Wheezing always means bronchospasm is the whole problem, so albuterol should be sufficient
This is cardiac asthma from fluid narrowing the airway walls in heart failure, so albuterol treats only part of the problem and CPAP and nitroglycerin address the underlying fluid
Albuterol is contraindicated in every patient with cardiac disease
Wheezing in this setting means she actually has COPD instead of heart failure
emt-medical-l11.why: Fluid in the airway walls from heart failure can cause wheezing, called cardiac asthma, so the wheeze does not prove pure bronchospasm and albuterol alone leaves the underlying fluid overload untreated. Albuterol is not broadly contraindicated in cardiac patients, and her neck vein distension, edema, and diuretic use point to heart failure rather than COPD.

emt-medical-l11.q: Which two history findings point toward acute heart failure rather than a COPD exacerbation as the cause of new shortness of breath?
choices: A productive cough that has changed color over several days
Recent weight gain of several pounds with new bilateral ankle swelling, and needing extra pillows or waking up gasping after lying down
A long smoking history and a barrel chest
Wheezing that started gradually over a week
emt-medical-l11.why: Rapid weight gain with bilateral edema, orthopnea, and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea are fluid-retention findings specific to heart failure. A changing productive cough, a smoking history with a barrel chest, and gradually worsening wheeze over days are more typical of a COPD exacerbation instead.

emt-medical-l11.q: A patient has sudden hypotension, distended neck veins, and clear lung sounds after no trauma. Which conditions belong on your differential for this combination?
choices: Massive pulmonary embolism, cardiac tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and right ventricular infarction
Asthma exacerbation and pneumonia only
Simple dehydration and orthostatic hypotension
Heat exhaustion and heat stroke
emt-medical-l11.why: Hypotension with distended neck veins and clear lungs in a non-trauma patient is a short, dangerous list of obstructive and cardiac causes: massive PE, tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and right ventricular infarction. Asthma and pneumonia would show abnormal lung sounds, dehydration typically causes flat rather than distended neck veins, and heat illness does not produce this specific triad.

emt-medical-l12.q: A patient has sudden double vision, slurred speech with normal word choice, and cannot sit up straight without falling to one side. Which stroke pattern does this fit?
choices: The five Ds of posterior circulation stroke: dizziness, diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia, and dystaxia
A classic anterior circulation stroke that FAST reliably catches
A simple inner ear problem with no stroke concern
A psychiatric event requiring no further workup
emt-medical-l12.why: Diplopia, dysarthria, and ataxia are three of the five Ds that flag posterior circulation stroke, which the standard FAST exam frequently misses since it does not test balance or vision. This combination is not benign inner-ear disease or a psychiatric presentation, and it is exactly the pattern anterior-circulation FAST screening is poor at catching.

emt-medical-l12.q: What is the purpose of applying a large vessel occlusion scale such as LAMS after a positive stroke screen?
choices: To decide whether the patient needs a glucose check
To predict a clot large enough that a catheter could remove it, favoring routing to a comprehensive stroke center capable of thrombectomy
To replace the need for a last known well time
To determine whether the stroke is hemorrhagic
emt-medical-l12.why: Scales like LAMS score findings such as facial droop, arm drift, and grip strength to estimate the likelihood of a large vessel occlusion, which helps route the patient to a center that can perform thrombectomy. Glucose checking and last known well are separate, still-necessary steps, and no field scale distinguishes hemorrhagic from ischemic stroke.

emt-medical-l13.q: A 3-year-old has a generalized seizure lasting 6 minutes with a temperature of 39.5 C, then has a second seizure an hour later. How should this be classified?
choices: A simple febrile seizure, since fever is present
A complex febrile seizure, because it is longer than 15 minutes or has recurred within 24 hours
Status epilepticus by definition, regardless of duration
Not a true febrile seizure since the child is older than typical
emt-medical-l13.why: A febrile seizure over 15 minutes, focal, or recurring within 24 hours is classified as complex rather than simple, and this one is both prolonged and recurrent. Status epilepticus is defined by continuous seizure activity or repeat seizures without regaining consciousness in between, which is not clearly described here, and age 3 falls within the typical 6-month to 5-year range.

emt-medical-l13.q: A patient had her last alcoholic drink 30 hours ago and has just had a brief generalized seizure. What does the timing suggest, and what should concern you next?
choices: This fits the 12 to 48 hour window for alcohol withdrawal seizures, and it is a warning sign for delirium tremens developing at 48 to 96 hours
This is too early for alcohol withdrawal and must have another cause
This confirms delirium tremens is already present
Alcohol withdrawal seizures only occur in the first 6 hours after the last drink
emt-medical-l13.why: Withdrawal seizures classically appear 12 to 48 hours after the last drink, and their appearance is a warning that delirium tremens, with its real mortality, may follow at 48 to 96 hours. This timing is textbook for withdrawal rather than being too early or already representing DTs, which has a distinct later-onset, more severe autonomic picture.

emt-medical-l14.q: A patient on an SGLT2 inhibitor is vomiting with deep rapid breathing, and her glucose reads 190. Why is this reading misleading?
choices: SGLT2 inhibitors can cause euglycemic diabetic ketoacidosis, so a near-normal glucose does not rule out DKA in these patients
The glucose meter is unreliable in patients on this medication
This glucose value proves DKA is not present
SGLT2 inhibitors always cause hypoglycemia, so this reading is unexpectedly high for her
emt-medical-l14.why: SGLT2 inhibitors dump glucose into the urine while ketones still build, producing DKA at a glucose that looks reassuring, so the vomiting and Kussmaul-pattern breathing must be judged on their own merits. This is not a meter malfunction, a normal glucose does not exclude the diagnosis in this drug class, and these drugs are not primarily associated with hypoglycemia.

emt-medical-l14.q: Why might glucagon fail to raise the blood glucose of a malnourished chronic alcoholic in hypoglycemia?
choices: Glucagon only works in patients under age 40
Glucagon releases stored glycogen from the liver, and a malnourished patient has little or no glycogen stored to release
Glucagon requires an intravenous route to work in alcoholics
Glucagon is destroyed by alcohol in the bloodstream
emt-medical-l14.why: Glucagon's mechanism depends on liver glycogen stores being available to convert to glucose, and chronic malnutrition or alcoholism depletes those stores, so the drug has little to work with. Age is not the limiting factor, glucagon is given intramuscularly or intranasally rather than requiring an IV, and alcohol does not chemically inactivate the drug.

emt-medical-l14.q: A patient with long-standing type 1 diabetes has no warning symptoms before her sugar drops and is first found confused with a glucose of 38 mg/dL. What does this describe?
choices: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state
A normal presentation with no special significance
Hypoglycemia unawareness, where the adrenaline warning system has stopped firing after years of diabetes
emt-medical-l14.why: After many years of diabetes, some patients lose the adrenaline-driven warning signs of low sugar, so confusion or a seizure becomes the first sign instead of shakiness or sweating, which is hypoglycemia unawareness. DKA and HHS both present with high, not low, glucose, and the absence of warning symptoms is a recognized and clinically important pattern rather than an unremarkable one.

emt-medical-l15.q: Two patients both have dilated pupils, a heart rate of 130, and elevated blood pressure. One has drenched, sweaty skin with active bowel sounds; the other has dry, flushed skin with a silent, distended abdomen. What distinguishes them?
choices: The sweaty patient with active bowel sounds fits a sympathomimetic toxidrome, and the dry flushed patient with a silent belly fits an anticholinergic toxidrome
Both patients have the identical toxidrome and the skin findings are irrelevant
The dry patient is a cholinergic poisoning
Pupil size alone tells them apart, and the skin findings do not matter
emt-medical-l15.why: Sympathomimetic and anticholinergic toxidromes look nearly identical on vital signs alone, so the skin and bowel sounds are what separate them: sweaty and active bowel sounds is stimulant, dry and silent is anticholinergic. Cholinergic poisoning instead produces pinpoint pupils and copious secretions, and pupil size here is identical between the two patients, so it cannot be the differentiator.

emt-medical-l15.q: A patient exposed to a pesticide has pinpoint pupils, is drooling and tearing, has wheezing lung sounds, vomiting, and a slow heart rate. Which toxidrome is this, and what is the mechanism of danger?
choices: Cholinergic toxidrome; the danger is bronchorrhea and bronchospasm drowning the patient in secretions
Sympathomimetic toxidrome; the danger is hyperthermia
Opioid toxidrome; the danger is respiratory depression alone
Anticholinergic toxidrome; the danger is urinary retention
emt-medical-l15.why: SLUDGEM-pattern secretions, wheezing, and bradycardia describe cholinergic toxicity, most dangerous because of bronchorrhea and bronchospasm filling the airway with fluid. Opioid toxicity causes pinpoint pupils too but without the drenching secretions and wheeze, and the sympathomimetic and anticholinergic patterns both feature dilated pupils rather than pinpoint ones.

emt-medical-l15.q: A patient started on a serotonergic antidepressant plus tramadol two hours ago now has agitation, tremor, diarrhea, and rhythmic beats of muscle when the ankle is sharply dorsiflexed. Which condition fits, and how does the timing help confirm it?
choices: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which typically also has a rapid onset like this
Serotonin syndrome, whose clonus and rapid hours-long onset after combining serotonergic drugs distinguish it from neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which builds over days with rigidity
Anticholinergic toxicity, since agitation and tremor are classic for it
This combination of findings has no recognized syndrome
emt-medical-l15.why: Clonus with brisk reflexes appearing within hours of combining serotonergic drugs is the signature of serotonin syndrome, unlike neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which develops over days and produces lead-pipe rigidity with sluggish reflexes instead. Anticholinergic toxicity does not produce clonus, and this presentation is a well-recognized, named toxidrome rather than an unclassifiable one.

emt-medical-l16.q: A patient who took a large amount of aspirin has ringing in his ears along with rapid deep breathing and sweating. What is the significance of the tinnitus?
choices: It is an unrelated finding and should be ignored
It only occurs in acetaminophen overdose
It always means permanent hearing loss has already occurred
It is an early, fairly specific clue to salicylate toxicity
emt-medical-l16.why: Tinnitus is a classic early warning sign of salicylate toxicity and should raise suspicion well before the more dramatic acid-base findings develop. It is not a feature of acetaminophen overdose, it is not an unrelated finding given the other symptoms, and it does not by itself indicate permanent hearing damage.

emt-medical-l16.q: A salicylate-poisoned patient is breathing rapidly and deeply. A well-meaning provider wants to sedate her to slow her breathing. Why is this dangerous?
choices: Her rapid breathing is a compensatory mechanism keeping her pH stable, and slowing it can cause the pH to drop and precipitate arrest
Sedation has no effect on salicylate patients either way
Rapid breathing in salicylate poisoning is unrelated to her acid-base status
Sedation would only cause mild drowsiness with no other risk
emt-medical-l16.why: The fast, deep breathing in salicylate toxicity is the body's own compensation for a mixed respiratory alkalosis and metabolic acidosis, so slowing it removes a protective mechanism and can cause a dangerous pH drop or arrest. This is exactly the mechanism the lesson highlights, not an unrelated or harmless effect of sedation.

emt-medical-l16.q: A patient who swallowed an unknown quantity of sustained-release verapamil two hours ago looks and feels completely normal. What is the correct disposition?
choices: Allow a refusal since she is currently asymptomatic
Transport regardless of how well she looks, because extended-release cardiac drugs can delay toxicity for many hours before causing shock
Observe her at home for 24 hours before deciding
Only transport if her heart rate drops below 60
emt-medical-l16.why: Sustained-release calcium channel blockers can look completely benign for hours before producing cardiogenic shock, so every one of these ingestions is transported regardless of the current exam. A refusal, home observation, or waiting for bradycardia to appear all rely on a deceptively normal window that this drug class is known for.

emt-medical-l17.q: A one-week-old infant has forceful, bilious, green vomiting. How should this be treated?
choices: As a surgical emergency, since bilious vomiting in an infant suggests malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise
As routine reflux, common in this age group
As a feeding intolerance that resolves with formula change
As pyloric stenosis, which is treated the same way
emt-medical-l17.why: Bilious, green vomiting in an infant is one of the fastest-killing pediatric emergencies because it suggests the bowel has twisted on itself, cutting off blood supply, and it needs urgent surgical evaluation. Reflux and feeding intolerance do not produce green vomit, and pyloric stenosis instead causes forceful but non-bilious projectile vomiting around 3 to 6 weeks of age.

emt-medical-l17.q: A 14-year-old boy reports sudden severe testicular pain but is reluctant to discuss it in front of his parents. Why must you ask about it directly and act quickly if suspected?
choices: Testicular torsion has only about a 6-hour window to save the testicle, and teenage boys commonly underreport it from embarrassment
Testicular pain in teenagers is almost always benign and rarely needs urgent evaluation
There is no time pressure since the testicle can be saved at any point
Only adult men, not teenagers, get testicular torsion
emt-medical-l17.why: Torsion has a narrow roughly 6-hour window before the testicle is lost, and embarrassment is a well-documented reason teenage boys delay reporting it, so directly asking about groin symptoms is necessary. This is not a benign, low-urgency complaint, and torsion occurs across a range of ages including adolescence, which is in fact when it peaks.

emt-medical-l17.q: A newborn who has been feeding well for weeks suddenly develops forceful, projectile, non-bilious vomiting at 5 weeks of age but is hungry again immediately afterward. What does this suggest?
choices: Pyloric stenosis, which classically appears around 3 to 6 weeks with this exact pattern
Intussusception
Malrotation with volvulus
A simple viral gastroenteritis
emt-medical-l17.why: Forceful, projectile, non-bilious vomiting with immediate hunger afterward at 3 to 6 weeks of age is the classic description of pyloric stenosis. Intussusception instead presents with episodic screaming and currant jelly stool, malrotation produces bilious vomiting, and a straightforward viral illness would not produce this specific hungry-right-after pattern.

emt-medical-l18.q: A woman has recurrent nosebleeds, heavy menstrual periods, and prolonged gum bleeding after dental work. She has no history of joint bleeding. Which bleeding disorder fits best?
choices: Hemophilia A, since it is the most common inherited bleeding disorder
Von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, which affects both sexes and causes mucosal bleeding rather than deep joint bleeds
Immune thrombocytopenia, which is always acquired rather than inherited
This pattern does not fit any recognized bleeding disorder
emt-medical-l18.why: Von Willebrand disease is actually the most common inherited bleeding disorder, affects men and women equally, and characteristically causes mucosal bleeding such as nosebleeds and heavy periods rather than the deep joint bleeds seen in hemophilia. Hemophilia is X-linked and overwhelmingly affects males with joint and muscle bleeding, and immune thrombocytopenia can be either acquired or associated with other conditions, though it is not the disorder described here.

emt-medical-l18.q: A sickle cell patient without her spleen functioning normally develops a fever of 38.9 C with no other clear symptoms. Why is this concerning?
choices: It is not concerning since sickle cell patients get fevers often and rarely need evaluation
Being functionally asplenic makes these patients especially vulnerable to serious bacterial infection, so any fever needs a sepsis workup
Fever in sickle cell disease is always due to a vaso-occlusive crisis and does not need further workup
Fever only matters if it is accompanied by joint pain
emt-medical-l18.why: Chronic splenic damage leaves sickle cell patients functionally asplenic and unable to fight certain bacterial infections effectively, so a fever alone is treated as a possible serious infection rather than something routine. It is not automatically explained by a pain crisis, does not require joint pain to matter, and should never be dismissed as low concern given this vulnerability.

emt-medical-l18.q: Which of the following are recognized triggers for a sickle cell vaso-occlusive crisis?
choices: Dehydration, cold exposure, infection, low oxygen, high altitude, and hard exertion
Only physical trauma
Only high altitude, with all other factors being irrelevant
Sickle cell crises occur randomly with no identifiable triggers
emt-medical-l18.why: Multiple stressors that increase sickling are well documented, including dehydration, cold, infection, hypoxia, altitude, and exertion, several of which are things an EMT can help mitigate in the field. Trauma alone is not the primary trigger list, altitude is only one of several triggers rather than the only one, and crises are not simply random.

emt-medical-l19.q: A patient on long-term prednisone develops sudden vomiting, abdominal pain, and hypotension that does not respond to fluid after a minor illness. What should you suspect?
choices: Adrenal crisis, because chronic steroid use suppresses the body's own stress response
A simple viral gastroenteritis with dehydration
An allergic reaction to her steroid medication
This presentation has no relationship to her steroid use
emt-medical-l19.why: Long-term steroid users cannot mount their own cortisol stress response during illness or injury, so an ordinary trigger can precipitate adrenal crisis with fluid-resistant hypotension. This is not typical simple gastroenteritis given the fluid-refractory hypotension, it is not an allergic reaction to her own medication, and her steroid history is directly relevant rather than incidental.

emt-medical-l19.q: A peritoneal dialysis patient reports abdominal pain and fever, and the fluid draining from her catheter looks cloudy instead of clear. What does this suggest?
choices: Peritonitis, an infection of the peritoneal cavity related to the dialysis catheter
A normal dialysis finding requiring no action
Disequilibrium syndrome
Hyperkalemia from a missed hemodialysis session
emt-medical-l19.why: Cloudy peritoneal dialysate with abdominal pain and fever is the classic sign of peritonitis, an infection that needs prompt evaluation, and the drained bag should be brought to the hospital. Disequilibrium syndrome and hyperkalemia are complications of hemodialysis rather than peritoneal dialysis, and cloudy fluid is not a normal, ignorable finding.

emt-medical-l19.q: A patient 8 days out from chemotherapy has one recorded temperature of 38.3 C with no other symptoms. Does she meet the threshold for a neutropenic fever emergency?
choices: Yes, a single temperature at or above 38.3 C, or 38.0 C sustained for an hour, meets the working threshold
No, a fever must be documented on two separate occasions before it counts
No, she needs a temperature above 39.5 C to qualify
Yes, but only if she also has an elevated white blood cell count
emt-medical-l19.why: The working definition is a single temperature at or above 38.3 C, or 38.0 C sustained for an hour, and at the white cell nadir around 7 to 10 days post-chemotherapy this single reading already qualifies as an emergency. Requiring two readings, a higher single threshold, or a documented elevated white count all describe thresholds this lesson explicitly does not use, since a neutropenic patient's white count is low, not high.

quiz.q: A patient in severe pulmonary edema is awake and cooperative, but his blood pressure is 76/48. What is the correct decision about CPAP?
choices: Withhold CPAP because hypotension is a contraindication; support ventilation and treat the shock instead
Apply CPAP and give a fluid bolus simultaneously
Apply CPAP immediately since it is first-line for pulmonary edema
Apply CPAP only at the lowest possible pressure
quiz.why: CPAP raises intrathoracic pressure and reduces venous return, which can worsen an already low blood pressure, so hypotension is a contraindication regardless of how appropriate CPAP would otherwise be for pulmonary edema. Using the lowest pressure still carries the same physiologic risk, and giving fluid does not change the contraindication.

quiz.q: A 58-year-old has three days of productive cough, fever of 38.7 C, pleuritic chest pain, and crackles heard only over the right lower lobe. What does the focal, one-sided finding suggest over a diffuse process?
choices: Pulmonary embolism, since PE causes localized crackles
Pneumonia, since the infection and consolidation are localized to one area
Congestive heart failure, since crackles are heard in one lung field early
Asthma, since wheezing is always focal
quiz.why: Fever, productive cough, and crackles confined to one lobe over days describe pneumonia, an infection filling alveoli in a discrete area. Asthma produces diffuse wheezing rather than focal crackles, pulmonary embolism classically presents with clear lungs, and heart failure crackles are typically bibasilar rather than isolated to one side.

quiz.q: A patient using an albuterol metered-dose inhaler correctly with a spacer develops a heart rate of 118 and a fine tremor a few minutes after the second puff. What should you do?
choices: Stop the treatment and treat this as an allergic reaction
Withhold all future oxygen since his heart rate is now elevated
Recognize this as an expected beta-2 agonist effect and continue monitoring
Give diphenhydramine to counteract the reaction
quiz.why: Tachycardia, tremor, and jitteriness are predictable systemic effects of a beta agonist working as intended and are not an allergic reaction. Diphenhydramine has no role here, stopping an effective treatment based on an expected side effect denies him needed bronchodilation, and his heart rate has nothing to do with his oxygen needs.

quiz.q: A teenager develops hives and swelling of the lips after a bee sting, with no breathing trouble and a normal blood pressure. Ten minutes later he starts wheezing and his blood pressure drops to 82/50. What changed about the diagnosis?
choices: Nothing; this was anaphylaxis from the first moment
This is still just a local allergic reaction since it started as hives
He has now progressed to anaphylaxis with a second and third system involved, meeting criteria that were not yet met initially
Anaphylaxis cannot evolve after the initial exposure
quiz.why: The initial picture with only skin involvement and normal vitals was a limited allergic reaction, but the addition of respiratory compromise and hypotension now meets the definition of anaphylaxis, showing that a reaction can evolve rapidly. It was not anaphylaxis from the start by the two-system-or-hypotension rule, it is no longer merely local, and reactions absolutely can progress after the triggering exposure.

quiz.q: Why is epinephrine effective for both the airway swelling and the low blood pressure of anaphylaxis in a single injection?
choices: Alpha-1 effects constrict blood vessels and shrink swelling while beta-2 effects open the bronchi, addressing both problems through different receptors at once
It works only on the airway and has no effect on blood pressure
It functions as a steroid that reduces inflammation over several hours
It works by blocking histamine receptors on mast cells
quiz.why: Epinephrine acts on multiple adrenergic receptors simultaneously, so alpha-1 stimulation raises blood pressure and reduces swelling while beta-2 stimulation relaxes the airway, unlike an antihistamine which blocks histamine receptors rather than using adrenergic pathways. It clearly affects blood pressure as well as the airway, and it acts within minutes through receptor stimulation rather than through a slow steroid-like anti-inflammatory mechanism.

quiz.q: What is the correct epinephrine auto-injector dose for a 22 kg child in anaphylaxis?
choices: 0.15 mg subcutaneously only
0.15 mg intramuscularly, the pediatric dose for a child under about 30 kg
1 mg intramuscularly
0.3 mg intramuscularly, the adult dose
quiz.why: At 22 kg, well under the roughly 30 kg cutoff, the pediatric auto-injector dose of 0.15 mg IM applies rather than the adult 0.3 mg dose. The route is intramuscular, not subcutaneous, and 1 mg IM is the cardiac arrest dose, not an anaphylaxis dose for any age.

quiz.q: About what percentage of strokes are hemorrhagic rather than ischemic?
choices: Less than 1 percent
About 87 percent
About 13 percent
About 50 percent
quiz.why: Roughly 13 percent of strokes are hemorrhagic, from a burst vessel, while the remaining approximately 87 percent are ischemic, from a clot; a CT scan, not field exam, distinguishes them. Fifty percent and under 1 percent do not match the recognized proportions for either type.

quiz.q: A stroke patient's last known well was 6 hours ago. Why is early stroke alert notification still worthwhile even though she is past the thrombolytic window?
choices: It is not worthwhile; nothing more can be done past 4.5 hours
Early notification only matters for the ambulance's own paperwork
Thrombolytics can still be given safely at 6 hours in all patients
Thrombectomy may still be an option out to 24 hours for a large-vessel occlusion, so early notification still matters for routing and preparation
quiz.why: Thrombectomy can extend treatment out to 24 hours in selected large-vessel strokes, so being past the thrombolytic window does not mean treatment options are exhausted, and early notification lets the receiving team prepare imaging and a possible intervention team. Thrombolytics are not safely given this late in general, and early notification has real clinical value, not just administrative value.

quiz.q: A 60-year-old has sudden vision loss in one eye and mild unsteadiness but a normal face, arms, and speech on the Cincinnati exam. Why should this still be treated as a possible stroke?
choices: BE-FAST includes balance and eyes specifically because posterior circulation strokes can spare the classic face, arm, and speech findings
Vision loss is never a stroke symptom
This can only be a migraine since the Cincinnati exam is normal
It should not; a normal Cincinnati exam rules out stroke
quiz.why: Balance and eye symptoms were added to BE-FAST precisely because posterior circulation strokes can leave the traditional face, arm, and speech exam normal while still being a true stroke. A normal Cincinnati exam does not exclude stroke, sudden vision loss is a recognized stroke symptom, and assuming migraine from a normal exam alone risks missing a treatable stroke.

quiz.q: A patient describes a headache that reached its worst intensity within seconds of onset, unlike any headache she has had before, with vomiting. What is the priority?
choices: Reassure her it is likely a migraine and let her rest at home
Treat this thunderclap presentation as a possible subarachnoid hemorrhage and transport urgently
Give her oral fluids and recheck in an hour
Have her lie flat with her head lowered to relieve the pain
quiz.why: A headache that hits maximal severity within seconds is the thunderclap pattern associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage and needs urgent transport, not reassurance or a wait-and-see approach. Lying flat with the head lowered can worsen intracranial pressure rather than help, and oral fluids do nothing for this presentation.

quiz.q: A patient seized for about 90 seconds with rigid muscles followed by rhythmic jerking, then stopped on his own. What is the correct interpretation of this duration?
choices: This is status epilepticus and needs immediate benzodiazepines
This duration means the patient was never truly unconscious
This is a typical generalized tonic-clonic seizure duration and does not by itself meet the definition of status epilepticus
Any seizure lasting over 60 seconds is abnormal and requires restraint
quiz.why: A generalized tonic-clonic seizure typically lasts about 1 to 2 minutes, so 90 seconds is within the expected range and does not meet the 5-minute status epilepticus threshold on its own. Restraint is never indicated for a seizing patient, and duration alone says nothing about whether consciousness was lost during the tonic-clonic event.

quiz.q: A patient had a witnessed generalized seizure 20 minutes ago and now has isolated left arm weakness that is gradually improving, with no other stroke findings. What does this most likely represent?
choices: Permanent neurologic damage from the seizure itself
Proof that the event was not a true seizure
A new acute stroke that requires no more consideration than routine transport
Todd's paralysis, temporary postictal weakness that can mimic a stroke and typically resolves over hours
quiz.why: Temporary one-sided weakness after a seizure, known as Todd's paralysis, is a recognized postictal phenomenon that resolves over hours and can look exactly like a stroke, though the patient still needs full evaluation since a true stroke cannot be excluded in the field. It does not represent permanent damage or disprove the seizure occurred, and it should not be dismissed as routine.

quiz.q: A patient with a glucose of 610 mg/dL is profoundly dehydrated and confused but has normal, unlabored respirations and no fruity breath odor. Which condition best fits, and what distinguishes it from DKA?
choices: Hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, which produces extreme hyperglycemia and dehydration without significant ketosis, unlike DKA
DKA, since the glucose is very high
This pattern is inconsistent with any diabetic emergency
Hypoglycemia, since confusion is present
quiz.why: HHS classically produces glucose values often above 600 with severe dehydration and altered mental status but without the ketone-driven Kussmaul breathing and fruity odor seen in DKA. Hypoglycemia would show a low, not high, glucose, and this pattern is a well-recognized diabetic emergency rather than something inconsistent with one.

quiz.q: After giving one tube of oral glucose to a hypoglycemic but awake patient, what should you do 15 minutes later if his glucose is still low and he remains symptomatic?
choices: Immediately begin high-flow oxygen instead of further glucose
Repeat the oral glucose and recheck again in another 15 minutes
Assume the glucose is inaccurate and stop treatment
Withhold further treatment since one dose has already been given
quiz.why: The rule of 15 calls for repeating a 15 g dose and rechecking every 15 minutes until the patient improves, so a still-low, still-symptomatic recheck calls for another dose rather than stopping. There is no reason here to distrust the meter, and oxygen does not address the underlying low blood sugar.

quiz.q: Which combination of findings is most typical of hypoglycemia rather than hyperglycemia?
choices: Warm, dry, flushed skin with severe dehydration
Polyuria and polydipsia developing over days
Pale, cool, sweaty skin with tachycardia, tremor, and hunger developing over minutes
Deep rapid breathing with a fruity breath odor developing over days
quiz.why: Hypoglycemia comes on within minutes and produces an adrenaline surge with pale, cool, sweaty skin, tremor, tachycardia, and hunger. Fruity breath, Kussmaul breathing, polyuria, polydipsia, and warm dry flushed skin with dehydration are all hyperglycemic patterns that develop over hours to days instead.

quiz.q: A patient with right upper quadrant pain radiating to the right shoulder blade after a fatty meal most likely has irritation of which organ, and why does the pain refer there?
choices: The pancreas, because pancreatic pain classically refers to the shoulder blade
The kidney, because flank pain always refers to the shoulder
The spleen, because splenic pain always refers to the right shoulder
The gallbladder, because shared nerve pathways send its pain signal to the shoulder blade
quiz.why: Gallbladder irritation classically refers pain to the right shoulder blade through shared nerve pathways, especially after a fatty meal that triggers gallbladder contraction. Kidney pain refers to the groin rather than the shoulder, splenic pain refers to the left shoulder rather than the right, and pancreatic pain classically bores straight through to the back rather than the shoulder blade.

quiz.q: A patient reports passing black, tarry, foul-smelling stool. What does this finding, called melena, typically indicate?
choices: Upper gastrointestinal bleeding that has been digested on its way through the bowel
Bleeding limited to hemorrhoids
Active, brisk lower gastrointestinal bleeding
A normal variant requiring no further evaluation
quiz.why: Melena describes blood from an upper GI source that has been altered by digestion as it passes through the bowel, producing the characteristic black, tarry, foul appearance. Brisk lower GI bleeding typically produces bright red blood per rectum instead, this is never a normal finding, and it is not specific to hemorrhoids, which usually cause bright red bleeding.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old has dull periumbilical pain that started this morning and has migrated over several hours to the right lower quadrant, along with loss of appetite and a low-grade fever. What does this classic migration pattern suggest?
choices: Testicular torsion, since abdominal pain can be the only symptom
Appendicitis, as the pain shifts from visceral midline discomfort to localized parietal irritation as inflammation progresses
A kidney stone, since pain commonly migrates
Gastroenteritis, which classically localizes to one quadrant
quiz.why: The classic appendicitis pattern is dull, poorly localized visceral pain around the navel that migrates to sharp, well-localized right lower quadrant pain as the inflamed appendix irritates the adjacent peritoneum. Kidney stone pain colics in waves toward the groin rather than migrating this way, gastroenteritis causes diffuse crampy pain rather than localized migration, and torsion should prompt a direct genital exam rather than being inferred from this abdominal pattern alone.

quiz.q: A patient who used cocaine an hour ago is agitated, sweating, with a temperature of 40 C and a heart rate of 158. What is the treatment priority?
choices: Restrain him prone to control his agitation quickly
Give naloxone since stimulants and opioids are treated the same way
Actively cool him, keep the environment calm, and take any chest pain seriously given cocaine's coronary risk
Withhold oxygen since his respiratory rate is already fast
quiz.why: Hyperthermia and cardiovascular collapse are the real dangers of stimulant toxicity, so active cooling and vigilance for coronary spasm-related chest pain are the priorities. Prone restraint risks positional asphyxia in an already compromised patient, oxygen should not be withheld based on respiratory rate alone, and naloxone has no effect on a stimulant.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient has slow shallow breathing and pupils that are normal in size rather than pinpoint. Naloxone produces no improvement. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The naloxone dose was too small and needs to be repeated many more times
The patient must not actually be in respiratory depression
This confirms the patient took a massive opioid overdose
A sedative such as a benzodiazepine, which naloxone does not reverse, is more likely than a pure opioid given the normal pupils
quiz.why: Normal-sized pupils and a lack of response to naloxone point away from a pure opioid toward a sedative like a benzodiazepine, which naloxone cannot reverse regardless of dose. Repeating naloxone endlessly will not help a non-opioid cause, a massive opioid overdose would typically still show pinpoint pupils, and slow shallow breathing is itself evidence of real respiratory depression.

quiz.q: Which pupil finding, paired with the vital sign trend, most quickly suggests an opioid rather than a stimulant overdose?
choices: Pinpoint pupils with a slow respiratory rate and low heart rate
Dilated pupils with a fast heart rate and high blood pressure
Dilated pupils with a slow heart rate
Pinpoint pupils with a fast heart rate
quiz.why: Pinpoint pupils together with slow breathing and a low heart rate are the fast bedside pattern for opioid toxicity, since opioids depress the respiratory and cardiovascular drive together. Dilated pupils with tachycardia and hypertension instead points toward a stimulant, and the mixed combinations of pinpoint pupils with tachycardia or dilated pupils with bradycardia do not match either classic pattern.

quiz.q: A child swallowed drain cleaner and has visible burns around the mouth. A bystander offers to give her milk to dilute it. What is the correct response?
choices: Induce vomiting first to clear residual caustic before considering dilution
Decline; diluting or neutralizing a caustic is avoided unless medical direction specifically directs it, and the priority is the airway
Accept the milk and give it right away
Give activated charcoal instead of milk
quiz.why: Diluting or neutralizing caustics is not a default action because it can worsen injury, and it is only done under specific medical direction, with the airway being the true emergency due to swelling. Activated charcoal is contraindicated for caustics because it obscures endoscopy without helping burns that have already occurred, and inducing vomiting re-exposes damaged tissue to the caustic substance.

quiz.q: What is the phone number for Poison Control in the United States, and within roughly what time window is activated charcoal most useful after an appropriate ingestion?
choices: There is no dedicated Poison Control number; call the hospital directly
1-800-222-1222, and within 24 hours of ingestion
1-800-222-1222, and roughly within 1 hour of ingestion
911 only, and within 4 hours of ingestion
quiz.why: Poison Control is 1-800-222-1222, a free line staffed by people who know substances better than most field providers, and activated charcoal is most effective when given within roughly an hour of an appropriate ingestion since its usefulness falls off quickly after that. There is a dedicated Poison Control line separate from 911 or the hospital, and charcoal's usefulness does not extend usefully out to 4 or 24 hours.

quiz.q: A firefighter pulled from a house fire is confused with normal-appearing skin color but a profound acidosis and worsening hypotension, despite an SpO2 reading of 98 percent. What should you strongly suspect in addition to carbon monoxide?
choices: A simple panic attack from the fire
A stroke unrelated to the fire exposure
Only carbon monoxide, since the SpO2 already explains everything
Cyanide toxicity from burning synthetic materials, since it causes collapse with normal-looking skin color and does not affect the pulse oximeter
quiz.why: Burning plastics, wool, and synthetic furniture release cyanide, which stops cells from using oxygen and causes rapid collapse with deceptively normal skin color, and a falsely reassuring SpO2 does not rule it out since it does not measure cellular oxygen use. This is not simple anxiety, an SpO2 reading tells you nothing about cyanide, and there is no reason here to suspect an unrelated stroke over the clear toxic exposure.

quiz.q: A patient is outdoors on a moderately hot, humid day and develops painful calf cramps after heavy sweating during yard work. He is alert with a normal temperature. What is this, and how is it different from heat exhaustion?
choices: Heat cramps, which occur with normal mentation and near-normal temperature, unlike heat exhaustion which adds pale, clammy skin and more significant systemic symptoms
Heat stroke, since any heat-related symptom on a humid day is heat stroke
Hyponatremic seizure activity
Heat exhaustion, since cramps always indicate exhaustion
quiz.why: Heat cramps are painful muscle spasms from salt and water loss with normal mental status and a normal or near-normal temperature, distinct from heat exhaustion's additional pale, cool, clammy skin, weakness, and mild temperature elevation. Heat stroke requires altered mental status with a significantly elevated core temperature, which is not described here, and there is no seizure activity in this vignette.

quiz.q: A patient has frostbitten fingers, and transport will take over an hour with no risk of refreezing along the way. What is the correct approach to rewarming?
choices: Immerse the hand in the hottest water available to speed rewarming
Do not rub or massage the tissue; if rewarming is appropriate, use circulating water around 99 to 102 F, then cover with dry sterile dressings and separate the digits
Rub the fingers vigorously to restore blood flow before covering them
Apply a direct dry heat source such as a hand warmer against the skin
quiz.why: Rubbing shreds ice-crystal-damaged tissue, so the correct method when rewarming is appropriate is controlled water in the 99 to 102 F range, with dry sterile dressings and digit separation afterward. A direct hot object risks burning numb, insensate tissue, and using the hottest available water rather than the specific controlled range also risks a burn injury.

quiz.q: A lightning strike hits a group of five hikers. Two are pulseless and apneic, and three are awake, moving, and moaning in pain. How should you triage this scene?
choices: Triage lightning victims exactly the same way as a mass casualty trauma incident, treating the walking wounded first
Treat the moaning, awake patients first since they are clearly in more distress

Treat the pulseless and apneic victims first, using reverse triage, since lightning arrests often respond to resuscitation while the moving victims are more likely to survive without immediate intervention
Declare the pulseless victims deceased immediately since multiple casualties make resuscitation impractical
quiz.why: Lightning arrests frequently respond to prompt resuscitation, which is the basis for reverse triage in this specific scenario: treat the apneic and pulseless first rather than the ordinary mass-casualty approach of treating the walking wounded first. Declaring pulseless victims deceased without attempting resuscitation ignores their comparatively good prognosis, and the awake, moaning victims are, by definition of reverse triage, the lower priority here.

quiz.q: A patient tells you she has thought about ending her life but has not decided on a specific plan. Why does asking about a specific plan matter for your risk assessment?
choices: A plan only matters if the patient has attempted suicide before
Asking about a plan is inappropriate and should be avoided
It does not matter; any suicidal ideation carries identical risk regardless of a plan
The presence of a specific plan and available means raises risk further, making this a more important detail to establish
quiz.why: A specific plan with available means is one of the factors that increases risk further beyond general ideation, so establishing whether one exists is a meaningful part of the assessment, and asking directly does not plant the idea. It is not inappropriate to ask, risk is not identical regardless of a plan, and a prior attempt is one risk factor among several rather than a prerequisite for a plan to matter.

quiz.q: An extremely agitated patient with apparent insensitivity to pain, unusual strength, and a temperature of 40.2 C has been struggling against three providers for several minutes. He suddenly goes limp and quiet. What should this change in your approach?
choices: Recognize this as a possible pre-arrest sign of excited delirium and intensify airway and cardiac monitoring immediately
Assume he is now safe to leave briefly unattended
Remove restraints immediately since he is no longer resisting
Relax monitoring since the struggle is over and he appears calmer
quiz.why: Sudden calm after a violent struggle in excited delirium is a recognized warning that cardiac arrest may be imminent, so monitoring should increase rather than decrease at exactly this moment. Removing restraints or leaving him unattended based on apparent calm ignores this risk, and relaxing vigilance is the opposite of the correct response.

quiz.q: A patient has a dialysis fistula in her left forearm. Where should you take her blood pressure?
choices: On the fistula arm, since it is closest and easiest to access
On the arm without the fistula or graft, since blood pressure, IV access, and blood draws are never done on the access arm
It does not matter which arm is used
On the fistula arm only if the thrill cannot be felt
quiz.why: The fistula or graft arm is never used for blood pressure, IV access, or blood draws because damaging it costs the patient their lifeline for dialysis, so the other arm is always used instead. It matters a great deal which arm is chosen, and the presence or absence of a palpable thrill does not change this rule.

quiz.q: A COPD patient's medication list shows only home oxygen and a rescue inhaler, while a different patient with similar shortness of breath takes furosemide, a beta blocker, and a potassium supplement. What does the second medication list suggest?
choices: An anticoagulant regimen, suggesting pulmonary embolism
Nothing different; both lists suggest the same diagnosis
Heart failure, since diuretics, beta blockers, and potassium supplementation are typical heart failure medications rather than COPD medications
COPD, since beta blockers are commonly used for bronchospasm
quiz.why: Furosemide, a beta blocker, and a potassium supplement are a heart failure medication pattern, while inhalers, home oxygen, and steroid rescue packs point toward COPD, so the medication list itself is a useful piece of history. Beta blockers are not used to treat bronchospasm, this list does not describe anticoagulation for a clot risk, and the two medication lists point toward different rather than identical diagnoses.

quiz.q: A 66-year-old reports needing three pillows to sleep and waking up gasping for air about two hours after lying down, along with 5 pounds of weight gain this week. What does this history suggest?
choices: A COPD exacerbation, since nighttime symptoms are typical of COPD
A pulmonary embolism, since sudden nighttime dyspnea always indicates a clot
Normal aging with no cardiopulmonary significance
Heart failure, since orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and rapid weight gain from fluid retention are classic heart failure findings
quiz.why: Needing extra pillows, waking up gasping after lying down, and rapid weight gain are the orthopnea, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea, and fluid-retention pattern specific to heart failure rather than COPD. A pulmonary embolism does not typically present with this gradual pattern of weight gain and positional symptoms, and this constellation is a significant clinical finding rather than something to dismiss as normal aging.

quiz.q: A previously healthy 29-year-old develops sudden hypotension, distended neck veins, and clear lung sounds with no trauma involved. Which of the following is on the differential for this combination?
choices: Massive pulmonary embolism causing obstructive shock
Uncomplicated asthma exacerbation
Dehydration from a viral illness
Simple vasovagal syncope
quiz.why: Hypotension with distended neck veins and clear lung sounds in a non-trauma patient is the signature of obstructive shock, and massive pulmonary embolism is one of the short list of causes including tamponade, tension pneumothorax, and right ventricular infarction. Vasovagal syncope and dehydration typically produce flat rather than distended neck veins, and asthma would show abnormal lung sounds rather than clear ones.

quiz.q: A patient has sudden vertigo, double vision, and a hoarse voice with normal facial strength and normal arm strength. Which stroke-related pattern do these findings fit together?
choices: A single random collection of unrelated symptoms
Three of the five Ds of posterior circulation stroke: dizziness, diplopia, and dysphagia or dysarthria-type findings
A classic FAST-positive anterior circulation stroke
Findings limited to a peripheral inner ear disorder
quiz.why: Dizziness, diplopia, and a hoarse voice or swallowing-related symptom line up with several of the five Ds used to recognize posterior circulation stroke, which a normal face and arm exam alone would miss. This is not simply an unrelated grouping of symptoms, it does not describe the classic anterior FAST-positive pattern, and dismissing it as inner ear disease ignores the neurologic pattern present.

quiz.q: A stroke screen is positive and the crew applies the Los Angeles Motor Scale, scoring facial droop, arm drift, and grip strength. What is the purpose of this second scale?
choices: To replace the need to determine last known well
To determine the patient's blood glucose without a meter
To help predict a large vessel occlusion and guide routing toward a comprehensive stroke center capable of thrombectomy
To decide whether the patient needs oxygen
quiz.why: Scales like the Los Angeles Motor Scale build on a positive stroke screen to estimate the likelihood of a large vessel occlusion, informing whether routing to a comprehensive stroke center for possible thrombectomy is appropriate. It has no relationship to oxygen therapy or glucose measurement, and last known well is still separately and always required.

quiz.q: A 2-year-old has a generalized seizure lasting about 5 minutes with a temperature of 39.3 C, and the parents report this is her first seizure ever, without any recurrence in the past day. How should this seizure be classified?
choices: Status epilepticus, since any febrile seizure over 4 minutes is automatically status epilepticus
Simple, since it was generalized, lasted under 15 minutes, and did not recur within 24 hours
Not a true febrile seizure since it is her first one
Complex, because any febrile seizure reaching 5 minutes is by definition complex
quiz.why: A febrile seizure is simple when it is generalized, lasts under 15 minutes, and does not recur within 24 hours, all of which describe this child; it is complex only if it is focal, lasts over 15 minutes, or repeats within 24 hours, so duration alone at 5 minutes does not make it complex. Status epilepticus is a separate threshold of 5 minutes of continuous seizure activity or repeat seizures without recovery, and being a first seizure does not exclude it from being a febrile seizure. Simple or not, the child is still transported so the fever source can be found.

quiz.q: A known epileptic patient's family reports she had a seizure this morning and then received a dose of home rescue intranasal midazolam about 10 minutes before your arrival. Why is this detail critical to report to ALS?
choices: Because ALS needs to know before potentially stacking another benzodiazepine dose, which raises the risk of respiratory depression
Because it determines whether she needs an ambulance at all
It is not important since rescue medications rarely affect further treatment decisions
Because it changes whether the seizure was truly epileptic
quiz.why: Stacking a second benzodiazepine on top of an already-given rescue dose without knowing about the first raises the risk of significant respiratory depression, so reporting the timing and dose is essential for safe further treatment. This detail does not reclassify whether the seizure was epileptic, and it certainly does not eliminate the need for transport.

quiz.q: A 24-year-old with type 1 diabetes and an insulin pump has been vomiting for several hours with abdominal pain. His glucose reads 275 and his breathing is deep and rapid. What should you suspect about his pump?
choices: The pump is functioning normally and is unrelated to this presentation
The pump delivery may have failed, since pumps use only rapid-acting insulin with no long-acting reserve, allowing ketoacidosis to develop within hours of interruption
The pump must be reprogrammed by the crew to correct his glucose
A bolus should be manually triggered from the pump to lower his glucose
quiz.why: Because pumps deliver only rapid-acting insulin without a long-acting depot, any interruption in delivery can lead to ketoacidosis within as little as 4 to 6 hours, which fits his vomiting, pain, and Kussmaul-pattern breathing. The pump is not something to assume is unrelated, and EMTs do not reprogram or trigger boluses from a patient's pump under any circumstance.

quiz.q: Why does glucagon often fail to help a severely malnourished, chronically fasting patient in hypoglycemia?
choices: Malnutrition destroys the injection site tissue needed for absorption
Glucagon works by directly adding glucose to the bloodstream, which malnutrition blocks
Glucagon releases stored liver glycogen into the blood, and malnutrition or chronic fasting leaves little or no glycogen available to release
Glucagon only functions in patients with type 2 diabetes
quiz.why: Glucagon's mechanism depends entirely on converting stored liver glycogen into glucose, so a patient with minimal glycogen reserves from malnutrition or prolonged fasting has little for the drug to act on. It does not add glucose directly itself, it is not restricted to type 2 diabetics, and tissue at the injection site is not the limiting factor.

quiz.q: What best describes hypoglycemia unawareness in a patient with many years of type 1 diabetes?
choices: A condition where blood sugar never drops low enough to cause symptoms
A permanent inability to develop hypoglycemia at all
A condition that only affects patients using insulin pumps
A loss of the usual adrenaline-driven warning symptoms, so confusion, seizure, or coma may be the first sign of a low blood sugar rather than shakiness or sweating
quiz.why: After many years of diabetes, the adrenaline warning response can stop firing, so classic early symptoms like shakiness and sweating are absent and the first sign can be confusion, a seizure, or coma. It does not mean the blood sugar avoids dropping low, it is not limited to pump users, and it does not prevent hypoglycemia from occurring at all, only from being felt in the usual way.

quiz.q: A patient has dilated pupils, a heart rate of 128, elevated blood pressure, and skin that is soaking wet with active, audible bowel sounds. Which toxidrome fits, and what excludes the anticholinergic pattern?
choices: Sympathomimetic toxidrome, because the drenched skin and active bowel sounds are the opposite of the dry, silent-abdomen picture of anticholinergic toxicity
Anticholinergic toxidrome, since dilated pupils and tachycardia are present
Opioid toxidrome, since altered vital signs are present
Cholinergic toxidrome, because of the diaphoresis alone
quiz.why: Dilated pupils and tachycardia occur in both sympathomimetic and anticholinergic toxicity, but drenched, sweaty skin with active bowel sounds points specifically to a sympathomimetic cause, while anticholinergic toxicity instead produces dry skin and a silent, distended abdomen. Cholinergic toxicity produces pinpoint rather than dilated pupils, and opioid toxicity produces slow breathing and pinpoint pupils rather than this picture.

quiz.q: A farm worker exposed to a pesticide has pinpoint pupils, is drooling, has wheezing lung sounds, and a heart rate of 48. Which toxidrome is this?
choices: Anticholinergic
Cholinergic, marked by pinpoint pupils, copious secretions, wheezing, and bradycardia
Serotonin syndrome
Sympathomimetic
quiz.why: Pinpoint pupils, drooling, wheezing from bronchorrhea and bronchospasm, and a slow heart rate together describe cholinergic toxicity from an organophosphate-type exposure. Sympathomimetic and anticholinergic toxicity both produce dilated rather than pinpoint pupils, and serotonin syndrome presents with clonus and hyperreflexia rather than this secretion-heavy, bradycardic picture.

quiz.q: A patient who started a new antipsychotic four days ago now has a temperature of 40.2 C, severe muscle rigidity, and sluggish reflexes. How does the multi-day onset help distinguish this from serotonin syndrome?
choices: Serotonin syndrome always takes longer to develop than neuroleptic malignant syndrome
A multi-day onset always rules out any toxidrome
Neuroleptic malignant syndrome typically builds over days, while serotonin syndrome typically develops within hours, so the slow onset favors NMS
It does not help; both conditions have identical time courses
quiz.why: Neuroleptic malignant syndrome characteristically develops over days after starting or increasing an antipsychotic, in contrast to serotonin syndrome's typical onset within hours of a serotonergic drug change, so this timeline supports NMS along with the rigidity and sluggish reflexes. The two conditions do not share an identical time course, a multi-day onset does not rule out a toxidrome altogether, and the relative speed described is the reverse of what is claimed in the fourth choice.

quiz.q: A patient who took an unknown quantity of a tricyclic antidepressant is drowsy on your arrival with a heart rate of 118 and a QRS of 150 ms on the monitor. What is the significance of a QRS this wide?
choices: It is a benign incidental finding unrelated to her ingestion
A QRS this wide always means she has taken too little of the drug to be dangerous
It indicates she needs oral activated charcoal rather than transport
Significant sodium channel blockade is present, predicting a real risk of seizures and ventricular dysrhythmia, so this patient needs rapid ALS transport
quiz.why: Tricyclic-induced sodium channel blockade widens the QRS in proportion to severity, and a QRS around 150 ms sits well past the 100 ms threshold that predicts seizures and approaches the 160 ms mark linked to ventricular dysrhythmia, meaning this patient is escalating and needs urgent transport with ALS. It is not incidental, a wide QRS does not indicate a small ingestion, and charcoal timing and appropriateness are separate from the urgent transport priority here.

quiz.q: An unresponsive patient has a heart rate of 42, blood pressure 80/50, and a glucose of 58 mg/dL. Which overdose best fits this combination of bradycardia, hypotension, and low glucose?
choices: Beta blocker overdose, since beta blockade impairs hepatic glucose release, producing a low rather than high glucose
Salicylate overdose
Calcium channel blocker overdose
Tricyclic antidepressant overdose
quiz.why: Beta blocker overdose classically produces bradycardia, hypotension, and low glucose because it blunts the liver's glucose release, distinguishing it from calcium channel blocker overdose, which causes the same bradycardia and hypotension but with a high glucose from blocked insulin release. Tricyclic overdose typically shows tachycardia with a widened QRS rather than this bradycardic picture, and salicylate overdose causes tachypnea and an elevated rather than depressed presentation.

quiz.q: A 16-year-old took an unknown number of extended-release verapamil tablets about 90 minutes ago and currently feels completely fine with normal vital signs. What is the correct disposition?
choices: Allow her to go home since she is asymptomatic at this time
Transport regardless of her current wellness, because extended-release cardiac drugs can delay serious toxicity for many hours
Have her return if symptoms develop over the next day
Transport only if her heart rate drops below 50 during your assessment
quiz.why: Extended-release calcium channel blockers are notorious for a deceptively normal window lasting hours before cardiogenic shock develops, so every one of these ingestions is transported regardless of how the patient currently looks. Sending her home, waiting for symptoms, or waiting for bradycardia to appear before transporting all rely on the exact false reassurance this drug class is known to produce.

quiz.q: A 9-month-old has episodes of drawing her knees to her chest and screaming intermittently, appearing entirely normal between episodes, and her most recent diaper had a small amount of blood and mucus. What is most concerning here?
choices: A normal variation in bowel habits
Colic, a benign and common condition in early infancy
Intussusception, given the episodic pattern and currant jelly stool
Ordinary teething discomfort
quiz.why: Episodic screaming with knee-drawing between periods of normal behavior, plus blood and mucus in the stool, is the classic intussusception picture and needs prompt evaluation. Colic does not produce bloody, mucus-containing stool, teething does not cause abdominal symptoms like this, and this pattern is well beyond a normal bowel variation.

quiz.q: A teenage boy is brought in with abdominal pain and is reluctant to mention any groin symptoms in front of his mother. Why is it important to ask directly and privately about testicular pain in this situation?
choices: Only adult men need to be asked about testicular symptoms
Boys never underreport genital symptoms, so this concern is unfounded
It is not important since testicular torsion is exceedingly rare in teenagers
Testicular torsion has roughly a 6-hour window to save the testicle, and embarrassment commonly causes teenage boys to underreport it, so a direct, private question can be lifesaving
