quiz.why: Torsion has a narrow time window before the testicle is lost, and the lesson specifically notes that teenage boys underreport it from embarrassment, making a direct, private question important rather than optional. Torsion is not rare in this age group, in fact it peaks in adolescence, and underreporting due to embarrassment is a documented pattern rather than something that never happens.

quiz.q: A 5-week-old has forceful, non-bilious, projectile vomiting immediately followed by wanting to feed again right away. What condition does this describe?
choices: Pyloric stenosis, which classically appears at 3 to 6 weeks with this exact pattern
Gastroesophageal reflux, a benign and common finding
Intussusception
Malrotation with volvulus
quiz.why: Forceful, projectile, non-bilious vomiting with the baby immediately hungry again at 3 to 6 weeks of age is the textbook description of pyloric stenosis. Intussusception instead causes episodic pain with currant jelly stool, malrotation causes bilious green vomiting, and ordinary reflux does not typically present as forceful projectile vomiting with immediate refeeding urgency.

quiz.q: A patient reports recurrent nosebleeds, heavy periods, and unusually prolonged bleeding after a tooth extraction, with no history of bleeding into joints. Which bleeding disorder does this pattern best match?
choices: Hemophilia A
Von Willebrand disease, the most common inherited bleeding disorder, which affects both sexes and causes mucosal bleeding rather than deep joint bleeds
Immune thrombocytopenia only
This description does not match a recognized bleeding disorder
quiz.why: Von Willebrand disease is actually the most common inherited bleeding disorder, occurs in both sexes, and produces mucosal bleeding such as nosebleeds, heavy periods, and prolonged bleeding after dental work rather than the deep joint bleeding of hemophilia. Hemophilia A is X-linked and overwhelmingly affects males with joint and muscle bleeding instead, this pattern is not specific to immune thrombocytopenia, and it does in fact match a well-recognized disorder.

quiz.q: A sickle cell patient who is functionally asplenic develops a fever of 38.6 C with no other symptoms yet. Why does this alone require urgent evaluation?
choices: It does not; sickle cell patients get frequent benign fevers
Fever in sickle cell disease is always caused by a vaso-occlusive crisis and needs no further workup
A functionally asplenic patient is especially vulnerable to serious bacterial infection, so fever alone is treated as a possible sepsis emergency
Fever only matters if accompanied by chest pain
quiz.why: Because sickle cell disease damages the spleen over time, these patients are functionally asplenic and cannot effectively fight certain bacterial infections, so fever alone is treated seriously rather than dismissed. It is not automatically a pain crisis, does not require an additional symptom like chest pain to matter, and should never be treated as routine or benign.

quiz.q: Which of the following is a recognized trigger for a sickle cell vaso-occlusive pain crisis?
choices: Only physical trauma
Sickle cell crises occur with no identifiable triggers
Cold exposure has no effect on sickling
Dehydration
quiz.why: Dehydration is one of several documented triggers for sickling, alongside cold, infection, hypoxia, altitude, and exertion. Trauma alone is not the sole trigger, cold exposure is specifically listed as a trigger rather than having no effect, and crises are not random or trigger-free events.

quiz.q: A patient on chronic prednisone therapy has sudden vomiting, abdominal pain, and a blood pressure that stays low despite a fluid bolus after a minor cold. What should you suspect?
choices: Adrenal crisis, since long-term steroid use suppresses the body's own stress response to illness
Simple viral gastroenteritis needing no special concern
An allergic reaction to her prednisone
A dialysis-related complication, even though she is not on dialysis
quiz.why: Chronic steroid use suppresses the body's own cortisol response, so an ordinary illness can precipitate adrenal crisis with hypotension that resists simple fluid resuscitation. This goes beyond typical gastroenteritis given the fluid-refractory hypotension, it is not an allergic reaction to her own long-term medication, and there is no dialysis history to invoke a dialysis-specific complication.

quiz.q: A peritoneal dialysis patient has abdominal pain, fever, and cloudy fluid draining from her catheter instead of the usual clear fluid. What does this suggest, and what should you do with the drained bag?
choices: This is a normal dialysis variation and the bag should be discarded
This suggests peritonitis, and the drained bag should be brought to the hospital for evaluation
This suggests hyperkalemia from a missed hemodialysis session
This suggests disequilibrium syndrome and needs no further action
quiz.why: Cloudy peritoneal dialysate with pain and fever is the classic sign of peritonitis, an infection that needs prompt hospital evaluation, and bringing the drained bag helps confirm the diagnosis rather than discarding it. Hyperkalemia and disequilibrium syndrome are hemodialysis-related complications, not peritoneal dialysis ones, and this is not a normal, ignorable finding.

quiz.q: A patient 9 days out from a chemotherapy cycle has a single temperature reading of 38.4 C and mild fatigue with no other findings. Does this meet the neutropenic fever threshold, and why might she lack the usual signs of infection?
choices: No, since she has no cough or localized pain, infection is unlikely
Yes, but only because her fatigue proves an infection is present

Yes, a single reading at or above 38.3 C meets the threshold, and at the white cell nadir around 7 to 10 days out she may lack pus, redness, or swelling because she has too few neutrophils to produce them
No, she needs a second confirmed high reading before any concern is warranted
quiz.why: A single temperature at or above 38.3 C already meets the working neutropenic fever threshold, and because chemotherapy patients hit their white cell nadir around 7 to 10 days post-cycle, they often lack the usual signs of infection like pus or redness since there are too few neutrophils to generate them. A second confirmatory reading is not required, absence of localized findings does not make infection unlikely in this population, and fatigue is not what defines the emergency, the fever threshold itself does.
